summary: Sorting is about ordering, but the interview value is the machinery around it: the merge step (two-pointer combine of sorted runs), partitioning (split around a pivot), counting (bucket by value when the range is small), and comparators (define 'order' for anything). Master the merge and partition routines and most sorting problems are variations — inversion counting, wave arrays, closest points, custom-key sorts.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Ask: is the value range small?
thoughtProcess.body: If values fit a small range (colors 0-2, digits, bounded ints), a counting/bucket sort is O(N + range) and beats comparison sorts. Reach for it before merge/quick.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. Reach for the merge step as a Swiss-army knife.
thoughtProcess.body: Merging two sorted runs with two pointers underlies merge sort, 'merge two sorted arrays', and inversion counting (count left-leftovers when a right element is taken). If a problem smells like 'combine sorted things' or 'count out-of-order pairs', think merge.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Partition when you need a pivot boundary.
thoughtProcess.body: Quick sort, partition-index, and Dutch-flag all rearrange around a pivot/value. Keep a boundary pointer and sweep. Watch the pivot placement and the <= vs < tie rules.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. When order is custom, write a comparator.
thoughtProcess.body: Largest-number (a+b vs b+a), factors sort, tens-digit sort, closest-points — the whole problem is defining the comparator. State the primary key and the tie-break explicitly, and cast to long when squaring/concatenating to avoid overflow.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Merge sort is stable; quick/heap are not — pick by tie-break needs.
thoughtProcess.body: When elements carry payloads and equal keys must keep input order, you need a STABLE sort. Merge sort is stable if the merge takes from the LEFT run on ties (A[P1] <= A[P2]). Quick sort and heap sort are unstable. In Java, Arrays.sort(int[]) is a dual-pivot quicksort (unstable, irrelevant for primitives), while Arrays.sort(Object[]) / Collections.sort use TimSort (stable). If stability matters, box to objects or hand-roll a stable merge.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Quick sort's worst case comes from the pivot, not the data.
thoughtProcess.body: A fixed pivot (first/last element) degrades to O(N^2) on already-sorted, reverse-sorted, or all-equal input because each partition peels off one element. Fixes: random pivot, median-of-three, or a 3-way partition for many duplicates. Recursion depth also becomes O(N), risking StackOverflowError; recurse on the smaller side and loop the larger to cap depth at O(log N).

thoughtProcess.title: 7. Before counting sort, pin down the value RANGE, not just N.
thoughtProcess.body: Counting sort is O(N + K) where K is the value range and needs O(K) space. It only wins when K is comparable to N. If A[i] can reach 1e9, a count[] of size 1e9 blows memory — fall back to a comparison sort. Handle negatives / non-zero minimums by offsetting the index with (value - min).

keyPatterns.name: Two-pointer merge
keyPatterns.when: Combine two sorted runs / count inversions

keyPatterns.name: Counting / bucket
keyPatterns.when: Values in a small bounded range
keyPatterns.template:
count[v]++ for all v
emit v, count[v] times, v ascending

keyPatterns.name: Partition around pivot
keyPatterns.template:
boundary i=0
for j: if A[j]<pivot swap(i,j), i++
swap pivot into i

keyPatterns.name: Custom comparator
keyPatterns.when: Order defined by a derived key

keyPatterns.name: Dutch-flag 3-way partition
keyPatterns.when: Three categories or a pivot with many duplicates (<, ==, > pivot)
keyPatterns.template:
low=0, mid=0, high=N-1
while mid<=high:
  if A[mid]<pivot: swap(low,mid); low++; mid++
  elif A[mid]>pivot: swap(mid,high); high--   // do NOT mid++
  else: mid++
examples: Quick sort partition with many equal keys

keyPatterns.name: Overflow-safe comparator
keyPatterns.when: Comparator subtracts keys that can be large or negative
keyPatterns.template:
// instead of (a,b) -> keyA - keyB  (can overflow int)
(a,b) -> Integer.compare(keyA, keyB)   // or Long.compare for long keys
examples: Any comparator where keys span the full int range

keyPatterns.name: Stable sort via composite key
keyPatterns.when: Need a tie-break that preserves original order or a secondary field
examples: Factors Sort (count asc, then value asc)
Tens Digit Sorting (tens asc, then value desc)

commonMistakes.title: Seeding max/answer wrong or overflow on keys
commonMistakes.wrong: int d = x*x + y*y;   // int overflow for large coords
commonMistakes.why: Squaring or summing large ints (coords up to 1e6, values up to 1e9) overflows int; cast to long before the arithmetic, and seed a running max from the first element, not 0, when negatives are possible.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting the all-zeros / leading-zero guard
commonMistakes.wrong: return concatenation;            // returns "000" for all zeros
commonMistakes.why: Concatenating sorted digits/strings without the guard returns things like "000" for an all-zero input; if the largest piece is "0", the whole answer is "0".

commonMistakes.title: Comparator returns a - b and overflows
commonMistakes.wrong: Arrays.sort(B, (a, b) -> a - b);   // a=2e9, b=-2e9 -> overflow, wrong order
commonMistakes.right: Arrays.sort(B, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a, b));  // or Long.compare
commonMistakes.why: Subtraction can exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE and wrap to a negative, so the comparator reports the wrong sign. Integer.compare / Long.compare branch internally and never overflow. With A[i] up to 2e9 (Largest Number, B Closest Points), a-b is unsafe.

commonMistakes.title: Inconsistent comparator -> 'Comparison method violates its general contract'
commonMistakes.wrong: (a, b) -> a.score >= b.score ? 1 : -1;   // never returns 0; not antisymmetric
commonMistakes.right: (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.score, b.score);   // 0 on equal, consistent sign
commonMistakes.why: TimSort validates a total order. A comparator that returns nonzero for equal elements, or whose sign isn't symmetric, throws IllegalArgumentException once the input is large enough to trigger a merge. Always return 0 on equality.

commonMistakes.title: In Dutch-flag, advancing mid after a high-swap
commonMistakes.wrong: else if (A[mid] > pivot) { swap(mid, high); high--; mid++; }
commonMistakes.right: else if (A[mid] > pivot) { swap(mid, high); high--; }  // re-inspect swapped-in value
commonMistakes.why: The element pulled from high into mid is unexamined and could be < or > pivot. Incrementing mid skips it, leaving the partition wrong. Only advance mid in the < and == branches.

commonMistakes.title: Using sqrt / double for distance comparison
commonMistakes.wrong: double d = Math.sqrt(x*x + y*y);   // slower, float rounding can misorder near-ties
commonMistakes.right: long d = (long)x*x + (long)y*y;   // sqrt is monotonic -> same order
commonMistakes.why: sqrt is monotonic increasing, so comparing squared distances yields identical ordering — the sqrt is pure overhead, and doubles lose precision on large coordinates and can flip near-equal points. Compare exact integer squared distance.

edgeCases: All elements equal (partition degenerates — watch <= vs < in the sweep).
Already sorted or reverse sorted (quick sort worst case O(N^2) with fixed pivot).
Single element or empty window (base cases in recursion / [B,C] with B==C).
Large coordinates/values — use long for squared distance and concatenations.
Duplicate keys with payloads — verify whether the required order is stable; merge sort keeps input order on ties only if the merge favors the left run (<=).
Counting sort with negatives or a large minimum — offset the index by (value - min); size the count array to (max - min + 1).
Counting sort when max value is huge but N is small (A[i] up to 1e9) — O(K) space is infeasible; use a comparison sort.
Quicksort on all-equal or already-sorted input with a fixed pivot — O(N^2) time and O(N) recursion depth; randomize the pivot or 3-way partition.
Comparator keys at the int boundary (values up to 2e9) — use long keys and Long.compare, never subtraction.
Odd-length wave array — the final element has no pair to swap; the loop bound i < N-1 must leave it in place.
